newsitem.title: THAILAND: IMF help seen painful, needed for Thailand.
newsitem.headline: IMF help seen painful, needed for Thailand.

text.p: Thailand needs to swallow its pride and seek outside help for its economy, analysts said on Monday.
Hit by its worst slump in more than a decade, Thailand badly needs the right help and borrowing from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) might be the most viable option, they told Reuters.

The stigma and strings attached to IMF loans have made Thailand reluctant to borrow. However, the magnitude of its problems and lack of foreign confidence in its remedial measures made outside help almost inevitable, they said.

"The time has come where nothing is sacrosanct any more for Thailand. The country has sacrificed so many sacred cows recently, I don't think it can resist the pressure to seek IMF help," said an executive of a major U.S. investment bank.
The permanent secretary of the finance ministry, Chatumongkol Sonakul, hinted on Monday that Thailand saw the IMF as a possible saviour.

"At the moment, the assistance we have from the IMF is purely technical. However, we do not rule out financial assistance from the IMF. The Bank of Thailand is looking at every avenue possible and it is up to them to make a decision," he told reporters.
An IMF team is already in Thailand helping authorities manage the flotation of the baht.

Thailand will need huge amounts of money to bail itself out of trouble. Its highly leveraged economy has hit a wall after a prolonged boom fuelled by rapid credit creation and heavy capital inflows. Local media reports have suggested between $10 billion and $20 billion as possible amounts of credit that may be needed by Thailand.
The country's problems have compounded because its currency has been overvalued, exports slumped and there was growing mismatch between central bank reserves and domestic liabilities.
At the heart of the problem was the crisis in the financial sector which was hit by high interest rates, lack of liquidity and rising poor quality of assets.
Analysts estimated that of about 4.5 trillion baht of total outstanding loans, more than 10 percent were non-performing.

On July 2, the central bank, in a move to break a deadlock caused by the fixed exchange rate on capital mobility and its high interest rate policy, cut loose its tightly controlled baht and allowed it to float.
Although Thailand has imposed several measures to contain the problems, the measures have yet to produce concrete results.

The baht has hit record lows and the stock market's recent brief rallies have petered out. The index ended down 2.65 percent on Monday at 611.91. Nicholas Bibby, economist at Chase Manhattan Bank in Hong Kong, said Thailand was likely to try its best to borrow via corporate means before resorting to the IMF's help because of conditions attached to any IMF programme.
But the question remains as to who has enough confidence to lend such large amounts of money to Thailand without ensdorsement from a body like the IMF.

A specialist in emerging Asian debt, Ismail Dalla, said Thailand was in need of a reputable organisation like the IMF to give its approval to a coherent programme to solve its economic woes and regain the confidence of foreign investors.
"What Thailand needs is a long-term standby facility from the IMF...an open credit line from the IMF that it can withdraw and use as needed," said Dalla, president of Washington Asset Management Inc.
"Thailand, compared to some other countries, is not in a desperate situation but it has lost credibility," he added.

If the IMF gave Thailand a credit line, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank would also chip in and there would be enough financial assistance on standby to help the country through its difficult times, he added.
Japanese monetary sources said on Monday any move by the IMF to help rescue Thailand would be key to Japan's participation in any multi-billion dollar Thai bail-out.
